case_name: Mehmet Nuri Özen and Others v. Turkey
court: The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section)

facts.text: The applicants are Turkish nationals.

anchor.surface_text: 5.  The applicants are Turkish nationals.

facts.text: They are all serving sentences in Turkish high-security prisons, where the authorities refused to dispatch their letters written in a language other than Turkish.

anchor.surface_text: 6.  They are all serving sentences in Turkish high-security prisons, where the authorities refused to dispatch their letters written in a language other than Turkish.

facts.text: At the time they lodged their applications, the applicants were serving their sentences in the F-type prison in Tekirdağ or the Bolu prison high‑security prison.

anchor.surface_text: 7.  At the time they lodged their applications, the applicants were serving their sentences in the F-type prison in Tekirdağ or the Bolu prison high‑security prison.

facts.text: On 14 January 2008 the Disciplinary Board at the applicant Mehmet Nuri Özen’s prison proceeded to check a letter he had written to another prisoner in Kurdish and decided to return the letter as they could not have it translated.

anchor.surface_text: 8.  On 14 January 2008 the Disciplinary Board at the applicant’s prison proceeded, in accordance with section 68 § 3 of Law no. 5275 on the execution of sentences and preventive measures (“Law no. 5275”), to check a letter the applicant had written to another prisoner in Kurdish. After reminding him that letters should in principle be written in Turkish, they informed him that they could not have the letter translated, for lack of staff, so they were unable to ascertain, as required under Rule 122 § 1 of the Regulations on prison management and the execution of sentences (“the Prison Regulations”), whether the content of the letter was “inoffensive”. They therefore decided to return the letter to the applicant.

facts.text: On 28 January 2008, the Bolu enforcements judge dismissed Mehmet Nuri Özen’s appeal against the decision to return his letter.

anchor.surface_text: 9.  On 28 January 2008, on the basis of the case file, the Bolu enforcements judge dismissed the applicant’s appeal against that decision.

facts.text: On 12 February 2008 the Bolu Assize Court dismissed Mehmet Nuri Özen’s appeal against the enforcements judge’s decision.

anchor.surface_text: 10.  On 12 February 2008 the Bolu Assize Court, also dismissed an appeal lodged by the applicant against that decision.

facts.text: On 21 and 26 September 2007 the Disciplinary Board decided to keep one letter written by each of the applicants Abdulkadir Uçar, Nezir Adıyaman, Canar Yurtsever and Erol Yılmaz in Kurdish, requiring translation at applicants’ expense.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  On 21 and 26 September 2007 the Disciplinary Board decided to keep one letter written by each of the applicants in Kurdish. Arguing that the prison had neither the staff nor the money to have them translated, they explained that the letters could be sent once they had been translated, at the applicants’ expense, by a sworn translator and their content had been found to be inoffensive.

facts.text: On 6 November 2007 the Tekirdağ enforcements judge dismissed an appeal lodged by the applicants Abdulkadir Uçar, Nezir Adıyaman, Canar Yurtsever and Erol Yılmaz against the decision to keep their letters.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  On 6 November 2007, based on the case file, the Tekirdağ enforcements judge dismissed an appeal lodged by the applicants.

facts.text: On 19 and 27 November 2007 the Tekirdağ Assize Court dismissed appeals lodged by the applicants Abdulkadir Uçar, Nezir Adıyaman, Canar Yurtsever and Erol Yılmaz against the enforcements judge’s decision.

anchor.surface_text: 13.  On 19 and 27 November 2007, based on the case file, the Tekirdağ Assize Court dismissed an appeal lodged by the applicant against that decision, having found no legal or procedural defect.

facts.text: On 10 October 2007 the Disciplinary Board decided to seize a letter written by Zafer Balcı to his mother in Kurdish because the prison staff did not understand Kurdish.

anchor.surface_text: 14.  On 10 October 2007 the Disciplinary Board decided, pursuant to section 68 § 3 of Law no. 5275 and Rule 91 § 3 of the Prison Regulations, to seize a letter the applicant had written to his mother in Kurdish. They explained that they had been unable to decipher the content of the letter because the prison staff did not understand Kurdish.

facts.text: On 22 November 2007 the enforcements judge dismissed Zafer Balcı’s appeal against the decision to seize his letter.

anchor.surface_text: 15.  On 22 November 2007, based on the case file, the enforcements judge dismissed an appeal lodged by the applicant.

facts.text: On 18 December 2007 the Assize Court dismissed Zafer Balcı’s appeal against the enforcements judge’s decision.

anchor.surface_text: 16.  On 18 December 2007, based on the case file, the Assize Court dismissed an appeal lodged by the applicant against that decision, having found no legal or procedural defect.

facts.text: On 2 May 2008 the Disciplinary Board decided not to send a letter Mehmet Nuri Tanış had written to his mother in Kurdish because they were unable to have it translated and understand its content.

anchor.surface_text: 17.  On 2 May 2008, the Disciplinary Board decided not to send a letter the applicant had written to his mother in Kurdish, because they were unable to have it translated and thus to understand its content and determine whether it was “inoffensive”.

facts.text: On 26 May 2008 the Disciplinary Board reached a similar decision concerning a letter Mehmet Nuri Tanış wrote to his sister in Kurdish.

anchor.surface_text: 18.  On 26 May 2008 they reached a similar decision concerning a letter written by the applicant to his sister in Kurdish.

facts.text: On 20 May and 18 June 2008 the Bolu enforcements judge dismissed Mehmet Nuri Tanış’s appeals against the decisions not to send his letters.

anchor.surface_text: 19.  On 20 May and 18 June 2008 respectively, on the basis of the case file, the Bolu enforcements judge dismissed the applicant’s appeal against those decisions not to send his letters, considering that the Board’s decisions were fully in keeping with section 68 § 3 of Law no. 5275 and Rule 123 § 1 of the Prison Regulations, as it had not been possible to determine whether the content of the letters matched any of the criteria set forth in section 68 § 3 of Law no. 5275.

facts.text: On 6 June and 11 July 2008 the Bolu Assize Court rejected Mehmet Nuri Tanış’s complaints against the enforcements judge’s decisions.

anchor.surface_text: 20.  On 6 June and 11 July 2008 respectively, basing itself on the case file, the Bolu Assize Court rejected the applicant’s complaint against these decisions, noting that the refusal to dispatch the letters had been based not on the fact that they were written in Kurdish but on the fact that their content was incomprehensible and therefore impossible to verify having regard in particular to the imperatives of order and security.

facts.text: On 10 October 2007 the Disciplinary Board decided to seize a letter Fevzi Abo had written in Kurdish because the prison staff did not understand Kurdish.

anchor.surface_text: 21.  On 10 October 2007 the Disciplinary Board decided to seize a letter the applicant had written in Kurdish, in conformity with section 68 § 3 of Law no. 5275 and rule 91 § 3 of the Prison Regulations, on the grounds that they had been unable to decipher the content of the letter because the prison staff did not understand Kurdish.

facts.text: On 20 November 2007 the enforcements judge rejected Fevzi Abo’s appeal against the decision to seize his letter.

anchor.surface_text: 22.  On 20 November 2007, based on the case file, the enforcements judge rejected the applicant’s appeal.

facts.text: On 18 December 2007 the Assize Court dismissed Fevzi Abo’s appeal against the enforcements judge’s decision.

anchor.surface_text: 23.  On 18 December 2007, based on the case file, the Assize Court dismissed an appeal by the applicant against that decision, finding that there had been no procedural defect or error of law.

facts.text: On 21 January 2008 the Disciplinary Board decided not to send a letter Engin Babayiğit had written in Kurdish because the prison had no staff to translate it and the prisoner refused to pay for translation.

anchor.surface_text: 24.  On 21 January 2008, relying on Rules 91, 122 and 123 of the Prison Regulations, the Disciplinary Board decided not to send a letter the applicant had written in Kurdish. They explained that the prison had no staff to translate the letter and took note of the prisoner’s refusal to cover the cost of translation himself.

facts.text: On 6 February 2008 the Kocaeli enforcements judge found the Disciplinary Board’s decision not to send Engin Babayiğit’s letter was in conformity with prison rules.

anchor.surface_text: 25.  On 6 February 2008, based on the case file, the Kocaeli enforcements judge found that the Board’s decision was in conformity with prison Rules 91, 122 and 123.

facts.text: On 28 February 2008 the Kocaeli Assize Court rejected an appeal lodged by Engin Babayiğit against the enforcements judge’s decision.

anchor.surface_text: 26.  On 28 February 2008, on the basis of the case file, the Kocaeli Assize Court rejected an appeal lodged by the applicant.

facts.text: On 2 May 2008 the Disciplinary Board refused to send a letter Ergün Karaman had written to his father in Kurdish because they could not understand its content and had no staff to translate it.

anchor.surface_text: 27.  On 2 May 2008, the Disciplinary Board decided to refuse to send a letter the applicant had written to his father in Kurdish, on the grounds that they could not understand its content and determine, as required by Rule 122 § 1, whether it was “inoffensive”. After pointing out that correspondence should, in principle be written in Turkish, they explained that they did not have any staff to translate the letter.

facts.text: On 20 May 2008 the Bolu enforcements judge dismissed Ergün Karaman’s appeal against the decision not to send his letter, noting the letter contained non-Latin characters and the right to correspondence was not unlimited.

anchor.surface_text: 28.  On 20 May 2008, noting that the letter in question contained characters which were not in the Latin alphabet, the Bolu enforcements judge dismissed the applicant’s appeal, pointing out that while the right to correspondence was guaranteed, it was not unlimited, and that in this particular case it was not possible to ascertain whether the content of the letter fell within the scope of the restrictions set forth in section 68 § 3 of Law no. 5275.

facts.text: On 10 June 2008 the Bolu Assize Court observed that the refusal to send Ergün Karaman’s letter was due to its incomprehensible content, not because it was written in Kurdish.

anchor.surface_text: 29.  On 10 June 2008 the Bolu Assize Court observed that the reason behind the decision not to send the letter was not the fact that it was written in Kurdish but the fact that its content was incomprehensible, making it impossible to carry out the verification provided for in section 68 § 3 of Law no. 5275.

arguments.claim: The applicants alleged that their right to respect for their correspondence under Articles 8 and 14 was violated by the refusal to dispatch their letters written in a language other than Turkish.

anchor.surface_text: Articles 8 and 14; The Court held that the applicants' right to respect for their correspondence under Article 8 was interfered with and that the interference was not in accordance with the law, thus violating Article 8.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that the refusal to send letters in languages other than Turkish interfered with the applicants' correspondence rights under Article 8 and was not lawful.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that the interference with prisoners' correspondence was justified, in accordance with the law, pursued legitimate aims such as preventing disorder and crime, and was necessary in a democratic society.

anchor.surface_text: The Government argued that, were the Court to find that there had been interference, the interference was justified under the second paragraph of Article 8. In their submission it was in accordance with the law, pursued a legitimate aim, namely preventing disorder and crime, and was necessary in a democratic society.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court concluded that no law or regulation envisaged restrictions on correspondence in languages other than Turkish, so the interference was not "in accordance with the law".

arguments.claim: The applicants submitted that there was no legal basis for prohibiting correspondence in a language other than Turkish and that the interference was arbitrary.

anchor.surface_text: In their submission the interference with their rights was therefore arbitrary as there was no legal basis for it.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that the interference was not "in accordance with the law" because no law or regulation prohibited correspondence in languages other than Turkish.

arguments.claim: The applicants argued that the ban on written communication in languages other than Turkish contradicted the practice of authorising oral communication in another language, indicating no legitimate aim was pursued.

anchor.surface_text: In their submission this ban on written communication was in contradiction with the practice of authorising oral communication in another language.

arguments.claim: The applicants criticised the authorities' refusal to examine the content of correspondence written in other languages, alleging it was based on an arbitrary assumption that such correspondence was potentially dangerous.

anchor.surface_text: They alleged that the authorities’ reluctance to examine the content of their letters was based on the arbitrary assumption that all correspondence written in another language was potentially dangerous.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court noted that the authorities refused to send letters not because of their content but because they could not understand them, which was not a lawful basis for interference.

arguments.claim: The applicants contended that expecting detainees to pay the cost of translation placed an excessive burden on them and was discriminatory compared to foreign prisoners.

anchor.surface_text: Expecting detainees to pay the cost of translations placed an excessive burden on them, and a burden which, in their submission, was not imposed on foreign prisoners.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court considered that the practice of requiring prisoners to pay for translation automatically excluded such correspondence from protection under Article 8.

arguments.claim: The applicants submitted that their mother tongue was Kurdish and that the Government failed to explain why letters in other languages were likely to jeopardise prison security or what preventive aim was pursued.

anchor.surface_text: They further submitted that the Government had failed to explain what criteria they had used, and why a letter written in a language other than Turkish and therefore incomprehensible to the authorities was likely to jeopardise prison security.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that the authorities did not base their decisions on any legitimate security grounds but on inability to understand the letters, which was insufficient justification.

arguments.claim: The Court held that some measure of control over prisoners’ correspondence is necessary and not incompatible with the Convention, but the interference must be based on content-related grounds prescribed by law.

anchor.surface_text: The Court notes, however, that the domestic laws governing such matters give an exhaustive list of the circumstances in which a letter written by a prisoner may be withheld from the addressee.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court emphasized that only correspondence threatening order or security or containing offensive content may be withheld under law.

arguments.claim: The Court found that the decisions not to forward the applicants’ letters were not based on any of the lawful grounds but solely on the authorities' inability to understand the language, thus lacking legal basis.

anchor.surface_text: Although they referred to section 68 § 3 of Law no. 5275 and Rule 91 of the Regulations on prison management and the execution of sentences to explain their decisions, it nevertheless remains – and the Government have acknowledged this – that the domestic authorities refused to send the letters not because their content failed to satisfy the above-mentioned requirements concerning security and the prevention of crime, but because the authorities concerned were unable to understand the letters.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court concluded that the interference was not "in accordance with the law" as required by Article 8 § 2.

arguments.claim: The Court concluded that the interference was not "in accordance with the law" and thus violated Article 8 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: The Court has already held that the mere monitoring of prisoners’ correspondence by the authorities amounts to an “interference” with their right to respect for their correspondence within the meaning of Article 8 (see, for example, Calogero Diana v. Italy, 15 November 1996, § 28, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996-V). This means that the actual content of the correspondence is immaterial in determining whether a restrictive measure constitutes an “interference”: what counts is whether the private correspondence was interfered with (see Frerot v. France, no. 70204/01, 12 June 2007, § 54).
